citation.title: Which Countries Send More Delegates to Climate Change Conferences? Analysis of UNFCCC COPs, 1995-2015
citation.venue_or_publisher: Foreign Policy Analysis, 16, pp. 478-491 (Oxford University Press on behalf of the International Studies Association)

question: Which factors determine how many delegates a country sends to the annual UNFCCC Conferences of the Parties (national delegation size, NDS), 1995-2015. The abstract names country resources, interest in mitigating fossil fuel emissions, vulnerability to climate change, interest group, civil society and bureaucratic influence, distance to the COP location, financial capacity, and Annex I versus non-Annex I status.
data: Not stated on the page available. The abstract gives the period (COPs 1995-2015) only. The sources, variables and sample size are not on the first page.
method: Not stated on the page available. The abstract says the paper examines the determinants of NDS, but the method, models and variable definitions are not on the first page.

definitions.definition: The page gives no formal definition. It uses NDS for the number of delegates a country sends to a COP, shown by counts of delegates per country.
definitions.quote: Eritrea and Trinidad and Tobago each sent only three delegates to the 2015 COP in Paris compared to Canada’s 287 delegates.

findings.claim: Authors state that country resources and interest in mitigating fossil fuel emissions are important determinants of delegation size. Here 'interest in the mitigation of fossil fuel emissions' is a country-level factor, not a count of fossil-fuel-linked delegates; the page does not say how it was measured.
findings.quote: The ﬁndings highlight a country’s resources and its interest in the mitigation of fossil fuel emissions as important determinants of its NDS.

findings.claim: Authors state that interest group politics matter more than civil society or bureaucratic influence for delegation size. The page does not define 'interest group' or say whether business is meant.
findings.quote: Interest group politics appear more important than civil society or bureaucratic inﬂuence in determining NDS.

findings.claim: Delegation sizes vary widely between countries and over time, for example for China.
findings.quote: the Chinese delegation ranged from 15 to 53 delegates at the ﬁrst fourteen COPs but from 88 to 334 at the 2009–2015 COPs.

findings.claim: Delegation size is at the member states' discretion (context for rules), and the authors cite literature that larger delegations give a state more voice at COPs.
findings.quote: NDS, which remains at the purview of member states,2 has been shown to signiﬁcantly affect states’ voice at COPs, as countries with larger delegations can better participate in numerous simultaneous negotiations

limitations.point: Only the first page of the published article (a one-page preview, about 506 words) was available. Data, method, definitions, results and limitations in the body of the paper were not read and are not recorded here.

The page does not define or identify 'business' or 'fossil-fuel linked' delegates or organisations. It concerns delegation size of countries, not the affiliation of delegates, so it gives nothing on Q1 or Q2 measurement.
Authors state that the determinants of delegation size had been little analysed before this paper, and that the evidence for a link with climate vulnerability is limited.
limitations.quote: Extant research underscores the importance of NDS, but it leaves the motivators of NDS underanalyzed.

limitations.point: The extracted file has an empty authors field and a title string that runs on into the affiliation; author names and year are taken from the title string and the copyright line. Peer-review status is not stated on the page. No instructions addressed to a reader or an AI were found.
